analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 40 senators including two committee leaders, never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Millions of Americans sign contracts—at work, on their phones, for credit cards—that force them to resolve disputes in private arbitration instead of court, and many also give up the right to join class actions. This bill would make such clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, restoring the right to sue in court and to join group lawsuits. It was introduced in April 2023 and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, and small businesses who would regain access to courts: people with discrimination, wage-theft, consumer-fraud, or antitrust claims could sue in a public courtroom and join class or collective actions, where shared legal costs make small individual claims viable.

how_it_helps.text: The bill voids predispute arbitration agreements for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, so companies cannot make suing in court a condition of taking a job or buying a product [S2][S3].
It also voids clauses that waive the right to participate in joint, class, or collective actions, restoring access to class-action litigation in court [S2][S3].

The definitions cover disputes regardless of whether the worker is classified as an employee or an independent contractor, and the law covers discrimination in employment, credit, housing, health care, voting, and public accommodations [S3].
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies to a given agreement, even if the contract purports to delegate that question to arbitration [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, banks, credit card issuers, tech platforms, and other companies that rely on arbitration clauses would face lawsuits in open court, including class actions, and likely higher litigation and settlement costs.

drawbacks.text: Defenders of arbitration argue it resolves disputes faster and cheaper than court for individual claims, and companies contend arbitration avoids the drawn-out class-action litigation this bill would restore [S2].

The bill applies to all new disputes from the date of enactment, so companies would face a sudden shift in litigation exposure and would have to rewrite contracts nationwide, including consumer terms of service and employment paperwork [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—restoring ordinary people's access to public courts, which arbitration clauses largely closed off—is substantial and wide-reaching, since arbitration clauses appear in most employment contracts and consumer agreements. The main cost falls on companies, which would absorb more litigation risk and expense; some of that could be passed to consumers, but the bill preserves arbitration for disputes where both parties agree after the fact and leaves collective bargaining agreements untouched.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate Judiciary Committee never held a hearing or voted on it, so it died when this Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on April 27, 2023, with 39 original cosponsors [S3].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Judiciary Committee on the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee took no further action—no hearing, no markup, no vote—and the bill received no floor vote in either chamber before the 118th Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on forced arbitration clauses in employment and consumer contracts keep the status quo: workers and consumers remain bound to private arbitration, avoiding the courtroom exposure and class actions this bill would have restored. The Supreme Court and federal law leave those clauses fully enforceable [S2].

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Forced Arbitration Injustice Repeal Act in the Senate [S3].

for.name: 38 Senate Democrats and 1 Independent
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Durbin, Whitehouse, Warren, Sanders, and Brown [S4].

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee leadership
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the two-year Congress, leaving it to die in committee [S5].

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority and minority floor leadership, 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and the Senate never took it up; without Republican support it could not have reached the 60 votes needed to clear a filibuster and reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 40 cosponsors were Democrats or allied Independents; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past its committee referral [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers and consumer-facing companies (banks, credit card issuers, tech platforms, gig platforms)
industries.note: These industries rely on predispute arbitration and class-action waivers to resolve disputes privately and cheaply; the bill would force them into open court and class litigation. From the public's side, arbitration clauses limit the ability of workers and consumers to enforce their rights, so the industry's interest in keeping them runs against ordinary people's interest in court access.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and alternative dispute resolution firms
industries.note: Private arbitration providers handle millions of consumer and employment cases annually; voiding predispute arbitration agreements for these dispute types would sharply shrink that market. Ordinary people generally do not choose this forum in advance, so providers' loss tracks the public's gain in court access.
